title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 3(p)
version: as amended, consolidated position widely cited as of 2024
text: Section 3(p) excludes from patentability an invention which, in effect, is traditional knowledge, or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of a traditionally known component or components. This is the primary statutory bar preventing a formulation or use that is already part of India's traditional knowledge (including Ayurvedic knowledge) from being patented, even if it has not been formally documented in a single prior-art publication.

title: Patents Act, 1970 — Section 3(d)
version: as amended, consolidated position widely cited as of 2024
text: Section 3(d) excludes from patentability the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance, and the mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance, unless it results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant. This provision is frequently confused with 3(p) but addresses a different problem — incremental modifications of already-known substances (notably in pharmaceutical 'evergreening') — rather than traditional-knowledge-derived inventions specifically. Keep the classifier and reasoning layer from conflating the two.
source_url: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/1398 (confirm exact wording against this primary source)
source_authority: Indian Patent Office / Ministry of Commerce and Industry
data_quality_note: Well corroborated (this is the provision at issue in the widely known Novartis v. Union of India Glivec litigation). Paraphrased, not verbatim — confirm exact wording before quoting.

title: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (as amended 2023) — Access and Benefit Sharing obligation
section: general (specific section numbers not verified — see note)
text: The Biological Diversity Act establishes a framework requiring that access to India's biological resources, and to associated traditional knowledge, for research or commercial use — particularly by foreign entities or non-Indian citizens — be approved by the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) or the relevant State Biodiversity Board, and that benefits arising from such use be shared on mutually agreed terms. The 2023 amendment and 2024 Rules adjusted the scope of what requires approval versus intimation, including easing some requirements for AYUSH practitioners and cultivators of registered/notified biological resources. The precise current thresholds (approval vs. simple intimation, exemptions for codified traditional knowledge) need confirmation against the amended Act and 2024 Rules directly — do not state a specific threshold to a user without that confirmation.
source_url: https://www.indiacode.nic.in (Biological Diversity Act, 2002) and https://nbaindia.org (NBA guidance) — confirm exact current section numbers and thresholds against these
source_authority: National Biodiversity Authority / Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

section_title: Ayurveda-Aahar as a distinct food category

title: TRIPS Agreement — Article 27.1 (patentable subject matter)
text: TRIPS Article 27.1 establishes that, subject to certain permitted exceptions, WTO member states must make patents available for inventions in all fields of technology, provided they are new, involve an inventive step, and are capable of industrial application. This is the international baseline against which India's own Section 3 exclusions (including 3(p)) must be understood — 3(p) is a permitted exclusion of subject matter that India considers not to be a genuine 'invention' at all (traditional knowledge), rather than a TRIPS-inconsistent carve-out of an otherwise-patentable invention.
data_quality_note: Article number and general substance are well established international IP law. Paraphrased, not verbatim — confirm exact treaty text against the WTO source before quoting.

title: Nagoya Protocol — Prior Informed Consent and Mutually Agreed Terms
text: The Nagoya Protocol to the Convention on Biological Diversity establishes the international framework requiring Prior Informed Consent (PIC) from the country/community providing genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge, and Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) governing how benefits from their use are shared. It is the international-law counterpart to India's domestic Biological Diversity Act and NBA approval process — an Ayurvedic product intended for international commercialisation may need to satisfy both regimes, and the jurisdiction toggle must make clear these are two distinct (though related) compliance obligations, not one.
data_quality_note: Well-established international instrument; effective date corroborated. Paraphrased summary, not verbatim treaty text.
